pages.name: The box
pages.text: A 3 by 3 matrix moves every point of space. Its columns are where i, j and k land. Here i and j stay on the floor, and k lands on `(1, 0.5, 2)`. The unit cube leans into a slanted box.

pages.name: Where j lands
pages.task: The matrix `[2 1 0; 0 3 1; 0 0 2]` moves space. Where does j land?
pages.why: Each column is where one arrow lands. Column 1 is where i lands, column 2 is j and column 3 is k. So read down column 2 to get `(1, 3, 0)`.

pages.name: The volume
pages.text: The floor is still the unit square. So the box's volume is its height, k's up part, 2. That volume is the [[determinant]]. It is the factor the move scales every volume by. Sliding k's tip sideways leans the box but keeps its height. So the volume stays 2.

pages.name: Read the height
pages.task: i and j stay on the floor, and k lands on `(2, −1, 3)`. What is the determinant?
pages.why: The floor is still the unit square, with area 1. The height is k's up part, 3. So the volume, which is the determinant, is 1 × 3 = 3.

pages.name: Flat
pages.text: As k's tip drops, the box gets lower and its volume falls. On the floor the box is flat, and the determinant is 0. All of space lands on that one flat plane. So the move cannot be undone. Push k's tip below the floor and the box comes out mirrored, with a negative volume.

pages.name: The recipe
pages.text: Take each top-row entry in turn. Cover its row and column. The 2 by 2 left gives its [[minor]], its ad − bc. With the signs + − +, the minors become [[cofactors]]. Multiply each entry by its cofactor and add them up. That gives 2 × 6 − 1 × 2 + 1 × 0 = 10. The box agrees. Its floor is the parallelogram of i and j, with area 2 × 3 − 1 × 1 = 5. Floor 5 times height 2 is 10.

pages.text: Put i, j and k in the top row as if they were numbers. Put a in row 2 and b in row 3. The same recipe gives a × b. Here it is 5k. Its dot product with a and with b is 0, so it stands square to both. Its length, 5, is the floor's area.

pages.text: A three-loop circuit's resistance grid is `[6 −3 0; −3 12 −3; 0 −3 6]`. Each diagonal entry is a loop's total resistance. Each shared 3 Ω becomes −3. The top-row recipe gives 6 × 63 − (−3) × (−18) + 0 × 9 = 324. It is not zero, so the grid does not squash space flat. That means exactly one set of loop currents fits, whatever the loop voltages.
